newsitem.title: ALBANIA: ALBANIAN LEADER FIGHTS FOR POLITICAL LIFE.
newsitem.headline: ALBANIAN LEADER FIGHTS FOR POLITICAL LIFE.

text.p: Albanian leader Sali Berisha is fighting for his political life after being forced to make huge concessions to rebels controlling nearly half the country in a bid to stave off their main demand, his resignation.

After trying to tough out the situation for weeks, Berisha bowed to pressure from abroad and from the increasingly well-armed rebels and agreed last weekend to form an all-party interim government and hold elections by June.

Reversing a long-time refusal to have anything to do with the ex-communist Socialist Party, the right-wing president picked Socialist Bashkim Fino, former mayor of the rebel-held southern town of Gjirokaster, as prime minister.
But the appointment, while representing a major concession by Berisha, failed to mollify rebel leaders in the south who continue to insist he must resign immediately.
The rebels, and many others across Europe's poorest country of 3.4 million, blame Berisha for not intervening over pyramid savings schemes that collapsed, bankrupting thousands of families.
However some Western diplomats fear the president's resignation at this point could make a bad situation worse.
"It could create an enormous power vacuum, and there does not seem to be anyone around who could fill it," one diplomat said. "It could further destabilise an already destabilised situation."

Analysts said a major reason for the breakdown of order, sparked by anger over the failed savings schemes, was lack of public confidence in the democratic institutions in a country that emerged from four decades of Stalinism only six years ago.

The parliament, dominated by Berisha's Democratic Party, is widely seen as discredited since it emerged from elections last year which were boycotted by the opposition and criticised as seriously flawed by international observers.
There is no real constitution in force to replace the communist-era one scrapped in 1990, only what are described as "constitutional dispositions" introduced in 1991 and 1992.

An attempt by Berisha to push through a new constitution in 1994, criticised by the opposition by giving the president too much power and failing to enshrine ethnic and religious rights, was rejected by the people in a referendum.

Some analysts believe one figure who could unite the country, at least for some time, is Socialist leader Fatos Nano, who has spent nearly four years in jail and is therefore untainted by the pyramid savings debacle.
Nano was convicted on corruption charges which the opposition said were politically motivated. Several countries, including Greece, have demanded his release.
Another figure with real stature is Albanian writer Ismail Kadare, who exiled himself to France in 1990 before the fall of communism.
Kadare warned earlier this week that his homeland risked committing suicide and called for international arbitration including the deployment of a multinational peacekeeping force.
However according to Albanian sources he has shown no inclination to date to become involved in politics.
Another possibility, however remote, would be a return of the monarchy, as proposed earlier this month by a small monarchist party, though there appears little popular support for this.

The heir to the throne, Leka Zogu, 57, fled Albania with his father King Zog in 1939 when only a few days old as Italian dictator Benito Mussolini sent troops to occupy the country. He currently lives in South Africa.
For Berisha and Fino, meanwhile, the task of restoring control over their divided country looks awesome.
The prospects of organising elections looks slim while nearly half the country is in rebel hands and the other half under a state of emergency.

And the rebels are refusing to hand back thousands of weapons looted from army barracks unless Berisha resigns, creating an explosive situation in a nation where traditionally grudges are carried through generations.
